passage: Monday: When Anirban walked into class, three girls by the window tittered behind their hands. His ears burned. He checked his shirt, his hair. At break he learned they'd been laughing at a cat video. Wednesday: Snickers came from the back row when he answered in English class, and again when he dropped his pencil. This time it was the same two boys, every time, eyes on him. Friday: He found a paper stuck to his bag: a drawing of him with huge ears. The two boys snorted as he pulled it off. Anirban took the drawing straight to Sangeeta Ma'am. She kept it, thanked him and spoke to both boys and their parents that afternoon.

qa.q: What had the three girls been laughing at on Monday?
qa.a: They had been laughing at a cat video.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when he found the drawing on Friday?
qa.a: He felt hurt and humiliated, and by then was sure the snickers were aimed at him, since the same boys kept targeting him.

qa.q: Why was taking the drawing to Sangeeta Ma'am the right step?
qa.a: The snickering had become repeated targeting with proof, so a trusted adult needed to know; she acted the same afternoon.

qa.q: How might the girls by the window have felt if Anirban had accused them on Monday?
qa.a: They would probably have felt confused and wrongly blamed, since their laughter had nothing to do with him.

grounding: Shows tittering that was an unrelated joke and snickering that was repeated targeting, and a child reporting the targeting to a trusted adult.

passage: Tejas, you think those boys are laughing at you. Sit, and let your Yusuf Nana tell you about my first night at the hostel in Aligarh. I was eleven. When the lights went out, I heard tittering from the beds across the room, and whispering, and more tittering. I lay stiff as a plank, sure they were laughing at my torn trunk and my village accent. By midnight I was ready to fight all of them. Instead, I sat up and said, “What's so funny?” A voice said, “Nothing. We're scared of the dark, so we're laughing instead of crying.” By morning, the four of us were friends. Still, Tejas, if it's the same boys every day, you tell your teacher.

qa.q: Where was the hostel?
qa.a: The hostel was in Aligarh.

qa.q: What was young Yusuf feeling as he lay stiff in bed?
qa.a: Young Yusuf felt hurt and angry, sure the boys were laughing at his torn trunk and village accent.

qa.q: What choice did young Yusuf make, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Yusuf sat up and asked what was funny instead of fighting, which showed the laughter was nerves, not mockery, and led to friendships.

qa.q: What was the first night like for the boys across the room?
qa.a: They were scared of the dark and laughing to keep from crying, not thinking about Yusuf at all.

grounding: Shows tittering that sounded like mockery but came from nerves, and the advice that repeated targeting should be reported.

passage: Jomon was halfway through his speech at the morning assembly when tittering started in the front rows. He faltered. Were they laughing at his accent? At the stain on his shirt? He couldn't stop and ask; four hundred students were watching, and the principal stood right behind him. His friend Gautam, by the stage steps, caught his eye and pointed up, quickly, twice. Jomon glanced back. A pigeon was strutting along the top of the banner, right above his head, bobbing in time with his words. Jomon grinned, took a breath and finished the speech. Afterwards Gautam said, “They were laughing at the pigeon, not at you.”

qa.q: What was strutting along the top of the banner?
qa.a: A pigeon was strutting along the top of the banner.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when the tittering started?
qa.a: He felt anxious and self-conscious, worried the students were laughing at his accent or his stained shirt.

qa.q: How did Gautam help Jomon keep going?
qa.a: Gautam quietly pointed up at the pigeon, showing Jomon the real cause of the laughter so he could finish calmly.

qa.q: What were the front rows actually laughing at?
qa.a: They were laughing at the pigeon bobbing above Jomon's head, not at him.

grounding: Shows a child hearing tittering during a speech and fearing mockery, when it was an unrelated joke, so assuming the worst is risky.

passage: I'm Nikita. When the scholarship results were read out, Aman put his head down on the desk and his shoulders shook. A couple of boys sniggered. “He didn't get it.” Varun, who sits beside Aman, didn't laugh and didn't guess. He just shifted his chair a bit closer and sat there, quiet, until Aman looked up. Then he asked, “You okay?” Aman wiped his face and laughed shakily. “I got it. I thought I wouldn't. My mum's going to cry too.” Varun grinned and clapped his shoulder. I don't know what Varun was thinking, but he was the only one who got it right.

qa.q: What was read out in class?
qa.a: The scholarship results were read out.

qa.q: What was Aman feeling when his shoulders shook?
qa.a: Aman was overwhelmed with relief and joy at getting the scholarship, not sadness, as the sniggering boys assumed.

qa.q: Why did Varun's approach work better than guessing?
qa.a: He offered quiet company and then asked, which let Aman share the real reason for his tears.

qa.q: How does Nikita view the moment?
qa.a: Nikita sees that the boys guessed wrong, and that only Varun, by waiting and asking, got it right.

grounding: Shows a child reading a crying classmate by offering quiet company and asking, rather than guessing, when the tears were relief.

passage: Monday: After PE, Mahima sat on the steps crying, fists clenched. Himani thought, She's hurt her ankle, and ran for the first-aid box. Mahima pushed it away. “I'm not hurt.” Himani didn't know what to do, so she just sat on the step beside her. After a while Mahima muttered, “They picked everyone except me. Again.” She was angry, not hurt. Wednesday: Himani noticed Mahima eating alone and joined her with her tiffin. They didn't talk about PE, just about a show they both liked. Friday: Himani was a captain. She picked Mahima first. Mahima's eyes shone, and this time nobody needed to ask why.

qa.q: What did Himani run for on Monday?
qa.a: Himani ran for the first-aid box.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling as she cried on the steps?
qa.a: Mahima was angry and hurt at being left out again, not physically injured as Himani first guessed.

qa.q: What did Himani do right after her first guess was wrong?
qa.a: She stopped guessing and simply sat beside Mahima, which gave her space to explain.

qa.q: What would change if Himani had laughed or walked away?
qa.a: Mahima would have been left alone with her anger, and the friendship might never have started.

grounding: Shows a child learning that a classmate's tears can mean anger rather than pain, and quiet company working better than guessing.

passage: Tushar, when your friend cried today, you froze. That's all right. Let your Pema Abi tell you what I learned in Gangtok, long ago. A girl in my class, Dechen, started crying in the middle of the maths lesson. Some laughed. I thought, Her mother must be ill; that was the saddest thing I could imagine. At break I sat beside her, not saying anything, just sharing my momos. After a while I asked, “Are you okay?” She said, “I read the question aloud wrong and everyone laughed. I'm so ashamed.” It wasn't sadness at all. If I had guessed out loud, I'd have made it worse. So I just sat. Sometimes that is enough.

qa.q: Where did young Pema go to school?
qa.a: Pema went to school in Gangtok.

qa.q: What was Dechen feeling as she cried in maths?
qa.a: Dechen felt ashamed and embarrassed after reading the question aloud wrong and being laughed at.

qa.q: What choice did young Pema make, and why did it help?
qa.a: She sat quietly, shared her food and then asked, instead of guessing out loud, which let Dechen say what was wrong.

qa.q: How might Dechen have felt about the classmates who laughed?
qa.a: Dechen probably felt more embarrassed and alone because of their laughter.

grounding: Shows a child reading a crying classmate by offering quiet company and asking, since the cause turned out to be embarrassment.

passage: Alka Teacher held up Hemant's torn geography book in front of the class. “Who treats books like this?” Hemant's eyes stung. He stared hard at the blackboard, blinking fast, jaw locked. Not here. Not in front of everyone. He asked to fetch water and walked out to the handpump behind the school, where the goats were tied. Alka Teacher found him there a few minutes later, splashing his face. She didn't mention the water on his cheeks. She said, “I spoke too sharply. Everyone cries sometimes, even teachers. You can sit here till you're ready.” Hemant nodded. “The goat ate the corner,” he said. Alka Teacher laughed, softly.

qa.q: Where did Hemant go after asking to fetch water?
qa.a: Hemant went to the handpump behind the school.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling as he stared at the blackboard, blinking fast?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and afraid of crying in front of everyone, so he fought back the tears.

qa.q: How did Alka Teacher help Hemant recover?
qa.a: She admitted she spoke too sharply, said everyone cries sometimes and let him stay by the handpump until he was ready.

qa.q: What might Alka Teacher have realised when she saw Hemant at the pump?
qa.a: She probably realised her public scolding had hurt him and that he needed privacy, not more attention.

grounding: Shows a child blinking back tears and leaving to hide them from classmates, and an adult normalising tears and offering a private space.

passage: On the morning her best friend moved to Bergen, Noa sat through reading time in the Oslo classroom with her book held high in front of her face. Her eyes kept filling. She blinked them dry, turned a page she hadn't read, blinked again. When a tear finally slipped, she asked to go to the bathroom and stayed a long time. Mr Anders Berg noticed the empty chair. When Noa came back, eyes pink, he knelt by her desk. “Missing Ingrid?” She nodded, not looking up. “Crying about that makes sense. The beanbag corner behind the shelf is yours whenever you need it today. No one will ask.” At lunch, Noa used it.

qa.q: Where did Noa's best friend move to?
qa.a: Her best friend moved to Bergen.

qa.q: What was Noa feeling as she held the book in front of her face?
qa.a: She felt sad about her friend leaving and afraid of being seen crying, so she hid behind the book.

qa.q: What did Mr Berg offer, and why did it help?
qa.a: He said crying made sense and offered the beanbag corner as a private space, which let Noa recover without being watched.

qa.q: What might Mr Berg have noticed that others didn't?
qa.a: Mr Berg noticed Noa's long absence and pink eyes, and connected them to her friend moving away.

grounding: Shows a child blinking back tears and going to the bathroom to hide them, and a teacher normalising tears and offering a private space.

passage: On his third night at the hostel, Gautam laughed along at dinner, then slipped away to the laundry room and sat behind the big dryers. He pressed his sleeve against his eyes so hard it hurt. If the boys saw, they'd call him a baby. Himani Ma'am, the warden, came in with a basket of towels and saw his shoes sticking out. She put the basket down and sat on an upturned bucket, a little way off. “The first week is the hardest. I cried every night in my first hostel,” she said. “You can sit here as long as you like. And you can phone home from my office tonight.” Gautam lowered his sleeve.

qa.q: Where did Gautam hide after dinner?
qa.a: Gautam hid behind the big dryers in the laundry room.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling as he pressed his sleeve against his eyes?
qa.a: Gautam felt homesick and sad, and scared the other boys would call him a baby if they saw him cry.

qa.q: How did Himani Ma'am make it okay for Gautam to cry?
qa.a: She shared that she had cried in her first hostel, let him stay in the private spot and offered a phone call home that night.

qa.q: What might the other boys at dinner have noticed?
qa.a: They probably only saw Gautam laughing along, not the homesickness he was hiding.

grounding: Shows a child hiding tears for fear of embarrassment, and a trusted adult normalising them and offering privacy and a call home.

passage: “Boooo! Butterfingers!” Santosh cupped his hands and yelled as the Green House goalkeeper let in another goal. Around them, the Red House kids joined in. Kavitha tugged his sleeve. “Santosh. Look at him.” “What? It's just a house match. They booed us last year.” “That was at the captains, and they were laughing too. Look.” The goalkeeper, a small Class 4 boy, stood with his gloves over his face. His knees were shaking. Santosh lowered his hands. “Oh.” “Cheer our team instead,” said Kavitha. Santosh thought, then shouted, “Well played, Red House! And good try, keeper!” A couple of kids looked at him oddly. The goalkeeper looked up.

qa.q: Which house was the goalkeeper from?
qa.a: The goalkeeper was from Green House.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when he lowered his hands?
qa.a: Santosh felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed, realising the booing was hurting a small, shaking boy.

qa.q: What did Kavitha suggest, and why was it better?
qa.a: She suggested cheering their own team instead, which kept the fun of rivalry without jeering at one scared player.

qa.q: What was the match like for the goalkeeper?
qa.a: The small goalkeeper was humiliated and shaking, hiding his face as the crowd booed each goal.

grounding: Shows booing that was friendly rivalry once turning into unkind jeering, and a child considering the target's feelings before joining in.

passage: I'm Ishita. At sports day last year, my friend Ganga was on the balance beam, and our whole class started chanting, “Cartwheel! Cartwheel! Cartwheel!” I was loudest. I thought we were helping. Ganga had told me that morning she wasn't sure about the cartwheel on the beam. She stood at the end with her arms out, and I saw her lip wobble. She did a small jump instead, and some kids went “Awww.” Afterwards she said, “You all made it so much harder.” I felt terrible. Now I cheer after someone finishes, not before, and I don't chant what I want them to do.

qa.q: What was the class chanting?
qa.a: They were chanting “Cartwheel! Cartwheel! Cartwheel!”

qa.q: How did Ishita feel after Ganga spoke?
qa.a: Ishita felt terrible, realising the cheering had pressured Ganga instead of helping.

qa.q: What did Ishita change, and why is it kinder?
qa.a: Ishita now cheers after someone finishes and doesn't chant demands, so the cheering supports rather than pressures.

qa.q: What was the balance beam like for Ganga with the chanting?
qa.a: Ganga felt pressured and scared, with the whole class demanding a move she wasn't sure about.

grounding: Shows group cheering putting pressure on a performer, and a child learning to consider the target's feelings before joining in.

passage: Quiz note, Friday. Deepika, Class 6. Today's inter-section quiz went well until the last round. When I made a terrible pun, Yash started a friendly “Boooo!” and the whole hall laughed, me included. That kind of boo is fun; everyone's in on it. But two minutes later, when Section C's youngest player got an easy question wrong, the booing started again, aimed at her. She shrank in her chair. Yash, I noticed, stopped at once and looked around. I paused the quiz and said, “Booing my jokes is fine. Booing a person who's trying is not.” After the quiz I spoke to the group who had kept going.

qa.q: What made the hall start a friendly boo?
qa.a: The teacher's terrible pun made Yash start a friendly “Boooo!”.

qa.q: What was the youngest player feeling when she shrank in her chair?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and hurt by the booing aimed at her after an easy mistake.

qa.q: How did Deepika make the difference between the two boos clear?
qa.a: Deepika paused the quiz and said booing her jokes is fine but booing a person who's trying is not, then spoke to the group afterwards.

qa.q: What might Yash have noticed that made the booing stop for Yash?
qa.a: Yash likely saw the young player shrink and realised this boo was aimed at a person, not a joke.

grounding: Shows booing as friendly fun in one moment and unkind jeering in the next, and considering the target's feelings.

passage: Yogesh, you shouted back at that boy today. Let your Binita Pishi tell you what I learned at your age. In our lane in Siliguri, a big boy called Montu started yelling at my little brother over a lost kite. His face was red, spit flying. Then he shouted, “Tomorrow I'll break your legs!” My brother froze. I wanted to scream back, and I was shaking. Instead I took my brother's hand, stepped back and walked straight home. I told our father everything, even the words about the legs. Baba went to Montu's house that same evening, and the next morning Montu came and said sorry to my brother.

qa.q: What was the argument about?
qa.a: The argument was about a lost kite.

qa.q: What was young Binita feeling when Montu shouted the threat?
qa.a: She felt frightened and angry, shaking and wanting to scream back.

qa.q: What choice did Binita make, and why was it safer?
qa.a: She stepped back with her brother, walked home and told their father everything, including the threat, so an adult could deal with it that evening.

qa.q: How might Binita's little brother have felt when she took his hand?
qa.a: He was probably still scared but relieved and safer with his sister leading him away.

grounding: Shows a child recognising angry shouting, stepping back instead of shouting back, and reporting a shouted threat to a parent.

passage: The power cut came just as Sumit and Chetan reached the fourth floor, and the stairwell went pitch dark. Sumit started yelling. “Why did you make us take the stairs? This is YOUR fault! Do something!” His voice cracked and bounced off the walls. Chetan's first instinct was to shout back. Then he heard Sumit's breathing: fast, ragged. He's not just angry. He's scared. Chetan kept his voice low. “Okay. Hold the railing. I've got my torch.” The little light came on. Sumit stopped yelling but was shaking. Chetan phoned the building guard, who came up with a big lamp and walked them both home.

qa.q: Which floor had the boys reached when the power cut came?
qa.a: They had reached the fourth floor.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling as he yelled in the dark?
qa.a: Sumit was frightened, as his fast, ragged breathing and cracking voice showed, even though it came out as anger.

qa.q: What did Chetan do that calmed things?
qa.a: He didn't shout back, spoke low, turned on his torch and phoned the building guard for help.

qa.q: What would change if Chetan had shouted back?
qa.a: Sumit's fear might have grown into a real fight in the dark stairwell, with no one getting help.

grounding: Shows a child recognising that a friend's shouting signals fear, staying calm instead of shouting back, and getting an adult.

passage: In the colony park in Pune, the cricket game fell apart when Abhinav threw down the bat and yelled, “NOBODY listens to me! I said the ball crossed the line!” He was red in the face, fists clenched. The others shouted back, and it got louder. Arohi stepped back from the crowd. She thought, He's angry, but he also just wants someone to hear him. She didn't shout. She walked to the bench where Mr Kulkarni, the building uncle who kept score, was sitting, and asked him to come. He listened to Abhinav first, then to the others. “Replay the ball,” he said. Abhinav picked up the bat, still sulking but quiet.

qa.q: Who kept score at the game?
qa.a: Mr Kulkarni, the building uncle, kept score.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when he threw down the bat?
qa.a: Abhinav was angry and frustrated, and also desperate to be heard after being ignored.

qa.q: Why was Arohi's choice safer than shouting back?
qa.a: She stepped back and fetched a calm adult, who listened to both sides and settled the dispute.

qa.q: How did the other players react to Abhinav's yelling?
qa.a: They shouted back, which only made the argument louder.

grounding: Shows a child reading a friend's shouting as anger and a wish to be heard, stepping back and getting an adult instead of shouting back.

passage: The clinic's waiting room was packed, the token number hadn't moved in an hour, and Nilesh's wrist throbbed in its sling. Beside him, his father, Chetan, let out a long, heavy sigh. Nilesh shrank. He's annoyed with me. I shouldn't have jumped off the wall. Another sigh, longer. Nilesh couldn't bear it. “Papa, are you angry I got hurt?” Chetan turned, surprised. “Angry? No. I was sighing because the doctor's message just came: the X-ray shows only a sprain, not a break.” He held up his phone. “That was a relief sigh. Two of them.” Nilesh let out his own breath. “I thought it was me.”

qa.q: What did the X-ray show?
qa.a: The X-ray showed only a sprain, not a break.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when his father sighed?
qa.a: Nilesh felt guilty and worried, sure his father was annoyed with him for jumping off the wall.

qa.q: What did asking achieve?
qa.a: It showed the sighs were relief about the X-ray, so Nilesh stopped blaming himself.

qa.q: What was the wait like for Chetan?
qa.a: Chetan was worried about the wrist and tired of waiting, and then relieved when the X-ray message came.

grounding: Shows a child reading a parent's sigh as annoyance at him, and asking to learn it was relief.

passage: In their Hyderabad flat, Pradeep brought his model volcano to the table where Amma was working. “Amma, can you help me with the lava?” Kalyani stared at her laptop and huffed, a short, sharp breath through her nose. Pradeep stepped back. She's fed up with me. I always ask at the wrong time. He turned to go. Then he stopped and asked, “Is that huff about me?” Kalyani looked up, surprised, then rubbed her eyes. “Oh, kanna, no. The internet just cut out in the middle of my meeting. For the third time.” She closed the laptop. “Ten minutes of lava. Then I'll try again.”

qa.q: What was Pradeep's model?
qa.a: Pradeep's model was a volcano.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when Kalyani huffed?
qa.a: Pradeep felt hurt and unwanted, thinking she was fed up with him for asking at the wrong time.

qa.q: Why was it good that Pradeep asked about the huff?
qa.a: Asking showed the huff was about the internet cutting out, so he didn't walk away blaming himself.

qa.q: What was the afternoon like for Kalyani?
qa.a: Kalyani was frustrated by the internet cutting out three times during her meeting.

grounding: Shows a child reading a parent's huff as annoyance with him, and asking to find a different cause.

passage: Nazia finished the last bar of the piece and looked up. Maria Miss let out a long sigh and closed her eyes. “Was it that bad?” Nazia asked, voice small. “Bad?” Maria Miss opened her eyes. “Why do you say that?” “You sighed. Like my brother does when I'm annoying.” “Ah.” She laughed. “No. That was a happy sigh. You finally played the tricky bit without stopping. I've been waiting three weeks to hear that.” “Oh.” Nazia's shoulders dropped. “I thought you were tired of me.” “Tired, maybe. It's my sixth lesson today. But never of you.” Nazia grinned and played it again.

qa.q: How long had Maria Miss been waiting to hear the tricky bit?
qa.a: She had been waiting three weeks.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when Maria Miss sighed?
qa.a: Nazia felt anxious and small, fearing the sigh meant the playing was bad or that Nazia was annoying.

qa.q: What did Nazia's question make possible?
qa.a: It let Maria Miss explain the sigh was happy relief, so Nazia stopped assuming Nazia was the problem.

qa.q: What did the sigh mean for Maria Miss?
qa.a: For Maria Miss it was a happy, tired sigh of relief that the tricky bit had finally been played right 🎶

grounding: Shows a child reading an adult's sigh as annoyance, when it was relief and tiredness, and asking before assuming.

passage: I'm Harsha, and on Saturday I went to Ojas's house. When Ojas told his grandmother he'd scraped his knee at football, she clicked her tongue three times: “Tch, tch, tch.” I thought she was cross with him, the way my coach tuts when we mess up. But Ojas didn't look worried. He just held out his knee. His grandmother shook her head slowly, face soft, and dabbed it with a cloth. “Tch, tch. Poor boy.” Later Ojas told me that in his house that sound means “oh, you poor thing.” I don't know what his grandmother was thinking, but it didn't sound like my coach's tut at all.

qa.q: What had Ojas scraped at football?
qa.a: Ojas had scraped his knee.

qa.q: What was Ojas's grandmother most likely feeling when she clicked her tongue?
qa.a: She most likely felt sympathy and concern for Ojas, as her soft face and “Poor boy” show, not disapproval.

qa.q: What could Harsha do next time a tongue-click seems cross?
qa.a: Harsha could look at the face and tone, or ask, before deciding it means disapproval.

qa.q: How did Ojas understand the sound?
qa.a: Ojas knew that in his house the sound means “oh, you poor thing,” so he wasn't worried at all.

grounding: Shows a tongue-click meaning disapproval in one setting and sympathy in another, and why a listener should not jump to conclusions.

passage: Monday: In their first week in Istanbul, Mohit asked the corner shopkeeper if he had mango juice. The man tilted his head back, raised his eyebrows and made a short “tsk.” Mohit's face went hot. He's annoyed with me. He left without buying anything. Wednesday: At school, his classmate Emre explained. “That's just ‘no’ here. Head back, tsk. It's not rude.” Mohit told his sister Bhavna. She laughed. “The bus driver did that to me! I thought he hated me.” Friday: Mohit went back and asked for orange juice. The shopkeeper nodded and smiled. When Mohit asked for a straw, he got a “tsk.” This time Mohit just smiled back.

qa.q: What did Mohit ask for on Monday?
qa.a: Mohit asked if the shopkeeper had mango juice.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when the shopkeeper made the “tsk”?
qa.a: Mohit felt embarrassed and hurt, thinking the shopkeeper was annoyed with him.

qa.q: What helped Mohit understand the sound?
qa.a: His classmate Emre explained that head back with a tsk simply means no there, so Mohit could stop taking it personally.

qa.q: What did Bhavna's story about the bus driver show?
qa.a: It showed she had made the same mistake, reading a plain no as dislike.

grounding: Shows a child learning that a tongue-click can mean a plain no in another culture, not disapproval.

passage: Saurabh, you just went “ch-ch” when your friend dropped his ice cream. So did I at your age, and it got me into trouble. Let your Parul Dadi tell you. We had just moved to Leicester, and I was nine. In the playground a girl fell and cut her lip. I ran over saying, “Ch, ch, ch,” the way my mother always did when someone was hurt. The dinner lady grabbed my arm. “Don't you tut at her! That's rude!” I didn't have the English to explain. I just cried. The next day my mother came in and told the teacher it was our sound for sympathy. After that the dinner lady would say, “Ah, your ch-ch,” and smile.

qa.q: Where had young Parul's family just moved?
qa.a: They had just moved to Leicester.

qa.q: What was young Parul feeling when the dinner lady scolded her?
qa.a: She felt shocked and upset, and helpless because she didn't have the English to explain her sympathy.

qa.q: What choice did Parul's mother make, and why did it help?
qa.a: She went in the next day and explained the sound meant sympathy, which cleared up the misunderstanding for good.

qa.q: How did the dinner lady first read Parul's “ch, ch”?
qa.a: The dinner lady heard it as a rude tut of disapproval, not knowing it was a sound of sympathy in Parul's family.

grounding: Shows a tongue-click meaning sympathy in one culture and disapproval in another, and a listener jumping to the wrong conclusion.

subtype: Hmm, uh and um as thinking sounds [Expressing]
passage: Friday. Naveen's diary. In the social science oral today, Damini Ma'am asked me why rivers are important for farming. I knew it, but my mouth said, “Umm… uh… hmm.” Last year Sir always said, “Next!” the second I said umm, and I'd go red. Today Damini Ma'am just waited. She looked out of the window like she had all day. The umms went on for a bit, and then my brain caught up: water for the fields, soil from the floods, and villages growing up beside them. She nodded and wrote something down. At the end she said, “Your umm means you're thinking. Keep thinking.” I got nine out of ten.

qa.q: What did Damini Ma'am ask Naveen?
qa.a: She asked why rivers are important for farming.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling while saying “umm” at first?
qa.a: Naveen felt nervous, remembering being cut off with “Next!” last year, even though the answer was there.

qa.q: Why did Damini Ma'am's waiting work?
qa.a: Waiting gave Naveen's thinking time to catch up, so the umms led to a full, correct answer.

qa.q: How did last year's Sir seem to read the umms?
qa.a: Last year's Sir seemed to read them as not knowing, cutting Naveen off instead of waiting.

grounding: Shows a child's umms and hmms as thinking sounds, and a teacher who waits getting a better answer.

subtype: Hmm, uh and um as thinking sounds [Expressing]
passage: At the village library under the peepal tree, Santosh Sir asked the children what the story's ending meant. Asif put up his hand, then said, “Hmm… uh… um.” Two older boys sniggered. “He doesn't know.” Santosh Sir held up one finger to them and turned back to Asif, waiting. The breeze rattled the leaves. A cow lowed somewhere.
